Article Title: In 2006, Google's senior VP emailed Steve Jobs seeking permission to hire a former Apple executive; Jobs replied: We would have a problem if...
Article Text:
In 2006, Google's senior VP emailed Steve Jobs seeking permission to hire a former Apple executive​

Steve Jobs wanted to know exactly what Jean-Marie Hullot would build in Paris

On 28 March 2006, Alan Eustace, then Google 's senior vice president of engineering, wrote an email that reads less like a hiring note and more like a request for royal assent. Google wanted to offer Jean-Marie Hullot, the French engineer who had been CTO of Apple 's applications division until the previous year, a job running a small engineering centre in Paris. Before anything moved, Eustace asked Steve Jobs for his blessing. Bill Campbell, Sergey Brin and Larry Page were on copy.The exchange, surfaced by Internal Tech Emails, goes well past politeness. Eustace noted that Hullot had agreed to abide by his non-solicit and non-compete terms, that he loved Apple, and would not do anything to hurt Jobs or the company. Then the part that has aged badly. Google's relationship with Apple mattered so much, Eustace wrote, that if the hire threatened it in any way, Google would pass on the opportunity. A rival CEO was being handed a quiet veto over Google's hiring.Jobs took eleven days to answer, and when he did, on 9 April, he asked a single question. What would Jean-Marie be working on? "We would have a problem if it is related to cell phone handsets, etc," he wrote.The timing explains the nerves. The iPhone was still nine months from being unveiled, and Hullot was among the people who had pushed hardest for Apple to build a phone in the first place.Satisfied with the answer, Jobs wrote back the next day that the arrangement would be fine with him.It did not hold. On 25 April, Eustace returned to say Hullot wanted to bring four engineers who had worked for him at Apple's Paris office, and offered to cancel the entire thing if Jobs objected. Jobs' reply the following day ran to nine words: Google should strongly prefer not to hire these guys. On 23 May, Eustace confirmed that Google would not open a Paris engineering centre at all. Hullot never joined. He built the photo startup Fotonauts, later Fotopedia, and died in 2019.These no-poach emails became evidence in a $415 million wage suppression caseThe thread entered the public record as a plaintiff's exhibit in In re: High-Tech Employee Antitrust Litigation, the 2011 class action in which roughly 64,000 engineers accused Apple, Google, Intel and Adobe of agreeing not to poach each other's staff to hold salaries down. Judge Lucy Koh rejected an initial $324.5 million settlement as too low and approved $415 million in September 2015, about $5,770 per worker.Tim Sweeney, reading it this week, needed two words: blatantly illegal.
Article Summary: In 2006, Google's senior VP emailed Steve Jobs seeking permission to hire a former Apple executive. Jobs wanted to know exactly what Jean-Marie Hullot would build in Paris. Google's relationship with Apple mattered so much, Eustace wrote, that if the hire threatened it in any way, Google would pass on the opportunity.

Article Title: Scientists say AI may soon help humans to talk to animals and birds, but the risk is ...
Article Text:
AI-generated image for representation

“One risk that is currently not taken into account in research ethics is the concern that we might be violating the privacy of animals by collecting data on their vocalisations and movements,”

“An interest in privacy is an interest in controlling how you appear to others, and the complex social lives of many nonhuman animals offer strong support for thinking animals have this interest.”

AI is decoding animal calls

“Hey! Come help!”,

“playback,”

“You can stress the animals. You can disrupt their social environment. You can pose conflicts between them, especially if you don’t really understand the meaning of the call,”

When communication becomes manipulation

The race to talk to animals

“Because AI is so fast, I have absolute conviction we will crack the code by 2030,”

What once seemed distant is becoming possible. Artificial Intelligence (AI) may soon help humans communicate with animals. But the technology is also raising an ethical question over whether animals have a right to privacy. Machine learning models are helping researchers catalogue and reproduce animal sounds, allowing scientists to identify patterns in how animals communicate. But researchers writing in Springer Nature warn that collecting and decoding these signals could itself raise ethical concerns.the researchers wrote.Machine learning is helping researchers sort large collections of animal sounds and identify patterns that can be difficult to detect manually. Biologist Vittorio Baglione, who has spent years studying carrion crow calls, said he was struck by how AI models could sort his recordings and identify common features in different calls.One call, which Baglione described as essentiallyis used by crows to summon others to defend a nest, he told Bloomberg.The ability to understand such signals could eventually make communication with animals possible. But researchers warn that the same technology could also be misused.One concern involvesthe practice of broadcasting recorded animal calls into the wild. A person could use an imitation of a familiar call to influence an animal’s behaviour without fully understanding what the signal means.Baglione warned that hunters or others with malicious intentions could misuse the technology.he said.César Rodríguez-Garavito, director of the More-Than-Human Life, or MOTH, Program at New York University, has also raised concerns about playback technology.In a 2025 report on AI systems for animal communication, Rodríguez-Garavito said the technology could expose animals to large numbers of people seeking to communicate with them or potentially allow the animals to be weaponised.Previous playback experiments have shown how distressing an artificial call can be. In 2007, zoologist Katy Payne acknowledged that she had caused an elephant significant distress after playing a recording of its dead grandfather’s voice.The example highlights the difficulty of using animal communication technology responsibly. A system may reproduce a call accurately without researchers fully understanding its meaning or the effect it could have on the animal.Despite those concerns, researchers and technology developers continue to pursue systems that could establish communication between humans and animals.There is currently a $10 million reward for a project that can establish communication with an animal without the animal recognising that it is communicating with humans.Private equity billionaire Jeremy Coller, who funds the Coller Doolittle Challenge, said at the challenge’s latest prize event in June that humans could reach the goal within the next decade.he said.If that happens, the technology could change how humans understand animal communication. It could also force researchers to consider whether understanding an animal’s signals gives humans the right to use information the animals may never have intended to share.
Article Summary: Machine learning is helping researchers sort large collections of animal sounds and identify patterns that can be difficult to detect manually. But researchers warn that the same technology could also be misused. A person could use an imitation of a familiar call to influence an animal's behaviour without fully understanding what the signal means.

Article Title: Apple iPhone 18 Pro, iPhone Ultra to launch on September 9: Likely specifications and price
Article Text:
Apple foldable iPhone (Representiave image)

Apple iPhone Ultra likely specifications and price

Feature Expected specification Inner display 7.8-inch OLED, minimal crease, liquid metal hinge Cover display 5.4 to 5.5-inch OLED, hole-punch camera Processor A20 Pro, 2nm, up to 18% faster than A19 Pro Memory and storage 12GB RAM, 256GB to 2TB Rear cameras 48MP main + 48MP ultra-wide, no telephoto Front cameras One per display, 18MP to 24MP Security Touch ID on the power button, no Face ID Battery Split cells, roughly 4,900mAh to 5,800mAh total Connectivity Apple C2 modem, MagSafe charging Build Titanium border, about 4.5mm open and 9mm closed Weight Around 229g to 240g Colours Silver or white, plus a near-black deep indigo Software iOS 27 with side-by-side multitasking Expected price $1,999 to $2,299 for 256GB, about Rs 1,76,000 to Rs 2,02,000 Higher configurations Up to $2,699 for 1TB, about Rs 2,37,000

Apple iPhone 18 Pro likely specifications and price

iPhone 18 Pro Expected specifications and price Display 6.3-inch LTPO+ OLED, Dynamic Island around 35% smaller Processor A20 Pro, 2nm, WMCM packaging Memory 12GB RAM Main camera 48MP with variable aperture Other cameras 48MP ultra-wide, 48MP telephoto with wider aperture Camera Control Revised, capacitive layer removed Battery 4,288mAh in most markets Connectivity Apple C2 modem, satellite 5G support Build Anodised aluminium, around 8.8mm to 9mm thick Colours Dark Cherry, light blue, silver, dark grey Expected price $1,299 to $1,399, about Rs 1,14,000 to Rs 1,23,000 Last year for reference iPhone 17 Pro started at $1,099

Apple iPhone 18 Pro Max likely specifications and price

iPhone 18 Pro Max Expected specifications and price Display 6.9-inch LTPO+ OLED Processor A20 Pro, 2nm Memory 12GB RAM Battery 5,567mAh, 5,391mAh in China Weight and thickness Around 240g, roughly 0.25mm thicker than the 17 Pro Max Main camera 48MP variable aperture, possibly exclusive to this model Camera plateau 11.54mm, up from 11.23mm Connectivity Apple C2 or Qualcomm modem depending on market Colours Dark Cherry, light blue, silver, dark grey Expected price $1,399 and up, about Rs 1,23,000 Higher configurations 1TB could rise by close to $300 over the 17 Pro Max

What more Apple is expected to launch at September 9 event

Apple will hold its "Surprise and Shine" event on Wednesday, September 9, at 10.30 pm IST at Apple Park in Cupertino, and this year the lineup breaks a pattern the company has followed for close to a decade. Three phones are expected on stage: the iPhone 18 Pro, the iPhone 18 Pro Max, and Apple's first foldable, which leaks have settled on calling the iPhone Ultra. The standard iPhone 18, the iPhone 18e and the second-generation iPhone Air have reportedly been pushed to spring 2027. That leaves the entire autumn lineup sitting at the expensive end of the range, with no cheaper model arriving a week later to take the pressure off.The event is also the first that John Ternus will host as chief executive, after taking over from Tim Cook on September 1, and he inherits an awkward pricing situation. Memory costs have climbed steeply through 2026, Apple has already raised prices on Macs and iPads in June, and the iPhone has so far been shielded from that. Most estimates now point to increases of Rs 9,000 to Rs 26,000 over last year's equivalents in dollar terms, with the foldable landing in a bracket no iPhone has occupied before.Preorders are expected on Saturday, September 12, rather than the usual Friday, which falls on September 11 this year, with retail sales starting Friday, September 18. India is expected to be part of the first wave for the Pro models, though foldable availability at launch is less certain.The iPhone Ultra is a book-style foldable that opens wider than it is tall, closer to an iPad mini cut in half than to the tall Android foldables sold here. Reports point to a 5.4 to 5.5-inch outer screen and a 7.8-inch inner display, a titanium frame, and a body around 4.5mm thick when open and roughly 9mm when shut. That is thinner than the iPad Pro and close to the thickness of a current Pro Max, which is the specific claim worth testing in person.Two things had to go to get there. There is no room for the Face ID module, so authentication moves to a Touch ID power button of the sort the iPad Air and iPad mini already use. There is also no telephoto lens, leaving a 48-megapixel main and a 48-megapixel ultra-wide on the back, positioned so they work whether the phone is open or shut. Both screens get their own front camera.Most of Apple's engineering effort has reportedly gone into the crease. A liquid metal hinge, ultra-thin glass, a structural glass mid-frame and an optically clear adhesive that fills micro-cracks over time are all in play, with a target crease depth below 0.15mm. The intent is not just an invisible crease out of the box but one that stays invisible after a year of folding, which is where every rival has struggled. A magnetic Apple Pencil was prototyped and reportedly dropped over concerns the tip would mark the inner display.Software is the other open question. iOS 27 is expected to bring side-by-side apps, iPad-style landscape layouts and sidebars, and beta code already references hinge angle detection, which suggests something similar to Samsung's Flex Mode. Apple has been pushing developers towards app adaptability for months. Whether third-party apps actually stretch properly on day one will decide how this phone reviews.The iPhone 18 Pro keeps the 6.3-inch size and the camera plateau introduced last year, so this is an internal upgrade rather than a redesign. Cases from the 17 Pro are expected to fit. The A20 Pro moves to a 2nm process and is tipped to be about 18 per cent faster and 30 per cent more efficient than the A19 Pro, with a wider memory interface and a larger cache for the efficiency cores.The camera change is the one that matters. The main sensor is expected to get a variable aperture, letting the phone stop down in harsh light and open up indoors, which is the first meaningful shift in iPhone exposure control in years. A three-layer stacked sensor is also rumoured, which would help with readout speed and low light. The Camera Control button is reportedly being simplified, with the capacitive layer removed after two years of complaints about accidental launches.The Dynamic Island is expected to shrink by around 35 per cent, from roughly 20.7mm to 13.5mm, though at least one leaker maintains that change has slipped to next year. Under-display Face ID, rumoured for a while, is not happening. Dark Cherry is the headline colour, alongside a light blue and silver, and leaked SIM trays suggest black may be missing from the lineup entirely.The Pro Max is where the battery gains land. A 5,567mAh cell would be nearly 10 per cent larger than last year's 5,088mAh unit, and paired with the 2nm chip and the more efficient LTPO+ panel, it should stretch what is already the longest-lasting iPhone. Units sold in China are expected to carry a smaller 5,391mAh cell because a physical SIM slot takes up room.That capacity comes with weight. The phone is expected to be about 0.25mm thicker and seven grams heavier at roughly 240 grams, with a camera plateau that grows from 11.23mm to 11.54mm. Some reports suggest the variable aperture camera may be exclusive to this model, which would be unusual but not without precedent, since the 15 Pro Max was the only phone in its year to get the tetraprism telephoto.Beyond the phones, Apple is expected to show the Apple Watch Series 12 with a ceramic case option returning, the Apple Watch Ultra 4, and the AirPods 5 with a new H3 chip. A smart home hub, a refreshed Apple TV and a new HomePod mini are all in the running as well, though those may be held for a smaller event later in the year. Software dates should be announced at the same time. iOS 27, iPadOS 27, watchOS 27 and the rest are expected to reach existing devices in the week following the event, with September 14 the most cited date.
Article Summary: Apple expected to unveil iPhone 18 Pro, 18 Pro Max and iPhone Ultra at September 9 event in Cupertino. The foldable is expected to have a 7.8-inch inner display and a 5.4 to 5.5-inch outer screen. The iPhone Ultra is a book-style foldable that opens to cut half the size of an iPad.

Article Title: Netflix unveils ‘VOID’, an AI model that can change a movie plot
Article Text:
Netflix

How Netflix VOID works



Netflix has unveiled an AI model that can alter the scene. While this is nothing new, Netflix’s model not just remove objects from video, it understands what should happen next, essentially altering the causality. Most object-removal technology leaves a gap where something used to be and/ or fills it with a plausible-looking background. VOID goes a step further: after erasing an object from a scene, it calculates how the surrounding environment should realistically respond to its absence, and in the process it adjusts the behaviour of other elements in the frame accordingly.The model, called VOID, is a vision-language system designed to edit video footage with a level of contextual awareness that sets it apart from several existing tools.For example, imagine this scenario: A movie director has just wrapped up a multi-million dollar action sequence where the star drives straight into a fiery, head-on collision. The cars explode, debris scatters, and the scene is a wrap.But suddenly, there is request to change the scene: The character survives and drive off into the sunset instead. This would mean costly reshoots or millions spent on computer-generated graphics.Netflix’s VOID can alter the scene and digitally erase the collision, the second vehicle, the smoke, and the flying debris. It will then generate new, realistic footage of pristine pavement, making it look as though the main character simply drove down an empty, peaceful road.The AI’s ‘magic’ lies in its grasp of real-world physics. Let us understand this by a different example. If a video shows a person jumping into a pool and splashing water onto the deck, VOID can completely erase the person. It will then intelligently alter the water and the wet concrete, leaving behind a perfectly still, undisturbed pool as if nobody had ever jumped in.“To train the model, we generate a new paired dataset of counterfactual object removals using Kubric and HUMOTO, where removing an object requires altering downstream physical interactions. During inference, a vision-language model identifies regions of the scene affected by the removed object. These regions are then used to guide a video diffusion model that generates physically consistent counterfactual outcomes,” Netflix said.“Experiments on both synthetic and real data show that our approach better preserves consistent scene dynamics after object removal compared to prior video object removal methods,” the company added.Netflix isn’t keeping this powerful tool locked behind studio doors, and made the VOID model available to the public on the AI platform Hugging Face, allowing anyone to download and use it.While there are already several video-altering tools on the market, such as Runway, DiffuEraser, and ProPainter, the Netflix team claims VOID is vastly superior, as per The Register.
Article Summary: Netflix has unveiled an AI model that can alter the scene. While this is nothing new, Netflix’s model not just remove objects from video, it understands what should happen next. The model, called VOID, is a vision-language system designed to edit video footage with a level of contextual awareness that sets it apart from several existing tools.

Article Title: Fraudster uses Raigad SP’s WhatsApp display photo to dupe police staff, seeks Rs 50,000
Article Text:
A cyber fraudster impersonated Raigad SP on WhatsApp, targeting police personnel for money transfers, but the scam attempt was foiled. (AI-generated image)





NAVI MUMBAI: Raigad Cyber Police have registered a case against an unidentified fraudster who allegedly used the WhatsApp Display Picture (DP) of Raigad Superintendent of Police (SP) Anchal Dalal to deceive several police personnel into transferring money.On Thursday, the fraudster sent a message to Raigad SP's reader, PSI Siddheshwar Murkute, asking him to transfer money urgently. Murkute immediately realised that it was a modus operandi commonly used by cyber scammers, as the WhatsApp message was sent from an international number that was not saved in his mobile phone.Thereafter, PSI Murkute learnt that the same scammer had sent similar messages to several Raigad police personnel. Fortunately, no one fell prey to the fraud, as the police personnel were aware of this modus operandi used by cyber fraudsters.Subsequently, PSI Murkute registered an FIR against the unidentified accused under the relevant section of the BNS for the offence of cheating by personation.The complainant, PSI Murkute, said, "I had received the WhatsApp message from an international number and the DP was of Raigad SP Anchal Dalal.The message read, 'I am in a meeting and my mobile is switched off. Immediately transfer Rs 50,000 to my bank account.' I knew the message sender was a scammer. I deliberately replied asking for the bank account number by pretending to send the money. As I received the bank account number from the scammer, it will be useful for the cyber police team to trace the bank account holder. "PSI Murkute added, "One police officer had received a WhatsApp message from the same international number asking to transfer Rs 2,000 by impersonating SP madam and claiming that it was required for filling diesel in the car, and that her mobile battery had drained and she was unable to pay online at the fuel station."API Amol Jadhav of Raigad Cyber Police said, "The cyber scammers use VPNs (Virtual Private Networks) to mask their identity. However, the Internet Protocol (IP) address of the WhatsApp number used by the accused will be obtained to trace the location, and the accused will soon be behind bars."
Article Summary: A cyber fraudster impersonated Raigad SP on WhatsApp, targeting police personnel for money transfers. Fortunately, no one fell prey to the fraud, as the police personnel were aware of this modus operandi used by cyber fraudsters. One police officer received a WhatsApp message from the same international number asking to transfer Rs 2,000 by impersonating SP madam.

Article Title: Smart Meters Bypassed To Steal Power, 14 Cases Detected In A Day In Khapri
Article Text:
Ai image

Nagpur:





Power thieves appear to have found a way to outsmart the smart meters, with the Maharashtra State Electricity Distribution Company Ltd ( MSEDCL ) detecting 14 cases of electricity theft in a single day in Khapri branch under Butibori sub-division.In all 14 cases, consumers allegedly bypassed the smart meters by tapping the incoming power cable, allowing them to draw electricity without the consumption being recorded. MSEDCL officials detected the illegal connections during inspections and are assessing the quantum of power stolen and the penalties payable in each case.Criminal and penal action is being initiated under Section 135 of the Electricity Act, 2003. The cases have prompted MSEDCL to intensify inspections across industrial, commercial and residential areas in Nagpur circle.Four cases were also detected in Shanti Nagar, while one each was reported in Bhutia Darwaja, Gandhibagh, Gondkhair, Bhiwapur, Chapegaon, Salwa and Gowari. Two cases were detected in Khapa.MSEDCL said it has adopted a zero-tolerance policy towards power theft, with flying squads and local officials tasked with detecting illegal connections.Officials are also monitoring connections disconnected for non-payment of dues to prevent unauthorised reconnection.MSEDCL Nagpur Circle chief engineer Rajesh Naik said illegal power use could cause short circuits, transformer failures and fires, endangering consumers and the distribution network. He urged citizens to use authorised connections and avoid inducements to obtain electricity through illegal means.
Article Summary: In all 14 cases, consumers allegedly bypassed the smart meters by tapping the incoming power cable, allowing them to draw electricity without the consumption being recorded. The cases have prompted MSEDCL to intensify inspections across industrial, commercial and residential areas in Nagpur circle.

Article Title: Meet Linus Chen-Plotkin, the 18-year-old Philadelphia student who analysed more than 600 works by Mozart, Beethoven, Haydn, and Schubert and found Mozart's melodies were less predictable
Article Text:
Pic courtesy: Society for Science/Chris Ayers Photography

Teen proves Mozart’s music is unpredictable

Meet Linus Chen-Plotkin

Pic credit: Society for Science/Chris Ayers Photography

Beyond the project

Mozart’s versatility is unparalleled, even today. Ever wondered what made him the ultimate musical architect, with every phrase perfectly placed and every note seemingly inevitable? Well, an 18-year-old from Philadelphia may have found the answer! Linus Chen-Plotkin analysed more than 600 classical compositions and discovered something that musicologists have debated for centuries but never quite quantified. Wolfgang Amadeus Mozart’s melodies are actually harder to predict than those of any other musician, including Beethoven and Schubert.For his Regeneron Science Talent Search project, Linus built three statistical tests to measure something he calls a melody's ‘memory’. His project, ‘Predictability and Statistical Memory in Classical Sonatas and Quartets’, was to find out how much earlier notes influence the ones that come after. The ‘memory’ tracks how much one note depends on the notes before it. High memory means earlier phrases keep influencing what comes next, making it more predictable. Low memory means the composer pivots quickly, keeping listeners slightly off-balance.The teenager ran these tests across 600-plus piano sonatas and string quartets by Joseph Haydn, Wolfgang Amadeus Mozart, Ludwig van Beethoven, and Franz Schubert.What he found was striking. Mozart's music had shorter memory across all three tests, which means his melodies broke patterns faster. They were less predictable. Mozart honoured classical form while constantly slipping something unexpected past the listener's ear. In other words, perfection in Mozart's case didn't mean predictability; it meant something far harder to achieve.Linus’ findings finally provide an answer to understanding Mozart's works. For centuries, critics have thrown around words like ‘genius’ and ‘innovation’ without pinning down what they mean. Linus gave us a way to climb closer to the answer. The unpredictability is what made Mozart the genius he was. An 18-year-old wrestler from Philadelphia picked up statistical tools and told us something new about how Mozart's mind worked. Perhaps Mozart would have enjoyed that twist.Born to Joshua Plotkin and Alice Chen-Plotkin, Linus hails from Philadelphia, PA. He is a student at the Germantown Friends School. He's a varsity wrestler and an advanced Mandarin student. He is not a classical music prodigy who spent his childhood at conservatories, but he knows its mathematics. During the statistical analysis, he approached classical music as a dataset. He saw centuries of musical tradition as raw material for mathematical investigation. He believes his approach and other quantitative methods can help improve the understanding of areas that are typically studied qualitatively. Think music theory, art history, and literature. All these fields have relied on interpretation for centuries, but Linus thinks they don't have to stay that way. Music is not really alien to him. In fact, he also sings and plays blues guitar at The Twisted Tail bourbon bar during his spare time. While he isn’t neck-deep in work, he doubles as a radio operator. Linus is also a licensed amateur radio operator and a former member and soloist of the Philadelphia Boys Choir & Chorale. Few people his age have taken so many different angles on the same art form!Linus isn't stopping at the musical memory. He plans to go beyond. He's collaborating with a Johns Hopkins professor on analysing the grammatical rules of rhyme and metre in Geoffrey Chaucer's medieval poetry. He will be using the same approach on poems that belong to different centuries. The question is almost the same. Can we measure what makes great writing work? How does a poem resonate with the reader? What makes the best works the best?
Article Summary: Teen proves Mozart’s music is unpredictable. Linus Chen-Plotkin analysed more than 600 classical compositions. His project, ‘Predictability and Statistical Memory in Classical Sonatas and Quartets’ was to find out how much earlier notes influence the ones that come after. Mozart's music had shorter memory across all three tests, which means his melodies broke patterns faster.

Article Title: In Japan, local authorities have installed signs warning drivers that cats may suddenly dash into the road, using playful illustrations to make the danger memorable
Article Text:
Japan installs playful signs to warn drivers about cats

The playful designs are based on a real danger for cats

Tsushima uses warning signs to protect an endangered wild cat

Japan combines warning signs with other wildlife protection measures

A simple warning becomes a memorable road-safety message

An unusual road-safety idea in Japan is turning an everyday danger into something drivers are unlikely to forget. In parts of the country, signs featuring cats warn motorists that an animal could suddenly run into the road. Some of the designs are deliberately playful, using striking cat illustrations rather than conventional wildlife-warning imagery. The idea is rooted in a genuine road-safety concern. Cats can suddenly enter roads while chasing birds or insects, and their sensitivity to noise and light can sometimes cause them to freeze when confronted by a vehicle. Organisations and local authorities have therefore used visual warnings to encourage motorists to slow down and stay alert. The approach has also been adapted for wildlife conservation, including efforts to protect Japan's endangered Tsushima leopard cat from road traffic.One of the most distinctive examples came from Yellow Hat, a Japanese automotive retailer that launched a road-safety campaign focused specifically on reducing cat traffic accidents. As part of the campaign, the company created a cat warning sign designed to catch drivers' attention and remind them that cats can suddenly enter the road.The design was developed with supervision from a Kyoto University animal psychology research team specialising in companion-animal behaviour. Rather than relying on a standard warning image, the sign attempted to recreate the expression and posture of a cat about to dash into the road. Yellow Hat said the aim was to create a warning that would be particularly effective at attracting attention. The campaign was launched around Cat Day in February 2022, with a sign installed near a school in Tokyo's Shibuya area.Behind the amusing appearance of these signs is a serious problem. Yellow Hat explained that cats can run into roads because of their natural hunting behaviour, particularly when they chase birds or insects. The company also highlighted another difficulty. Cats are highly sensitive to sounds and light, and when confronted by a vehicle they can sometimes become unable to move instead of escaping from the road. That combination can create dangerous situations for both animals and motorists. The campaign therefore encouraged drivers to pay attention to cats while driving and to approach areas where animals may be present with greater care. The unusual artwork was intended to make the warning stand out rather than disappear among the many conventional signs motorists encounter on roads.The same basic idea becomes even more important on Tsushima, an island in southwestern Japan that is home to the critically endangered Tsushima leopard cat. Japan's Environment Ministry has repeatedly used warning signs and other measures to reduce vehicle collisions involving the species. The Tsushima Wildlife Conservation Center has installed warning boards near areas where leopard cats are known to occur or where previous accidents have happened. In one documented effort, authorities and local partners installed signs around an area with a history of leopard-cat traffic accidents, including signs designed to reflect vehicle headlights at night. Drivers are encouraged to slow down and remain alert, particularly because the animals are active around roads and can suddenly appear in the path of vehicles.The signs are only one part of a broader strategy. On Tsushima, conservation authorities have also used speed warnings, road markings, fencing, under-road passages and other measures intended to reduce the likelihood of animals entering traffic. The Environment Ministry says road accidents remain one of the most serious threats facing the Tsushima leopard cat, whose population is estimated at around 100 individuals. Historical records have documented numerous traffic-related deaths, while officials continue to run awareness campaigns and monitor accident hotspots. In 2024, the Environment Ministry also conducted a road-safety campaign after a leopard cat was killed during the daytime, highlighting that drivers should not assume the animals are only a nighttime concern.What makes Japan's cat-warning signs particularly striking is the way they combine a serious safety message with an approachable visual style. Instead of presenting wildlife as an abstract road hazard, the signs put the animal itself at the centre of the warning. That can make drivers more likely to notice and remember the message, especially when the artwork is unusual enough to stand out from conventional road signage. But the signs should not be mistaken for evidence of a single nationwide programme requiring cat-warning signs on Japanese roads. They represent different local and organisational efforts, ranging from campaigns aimed at ordinary domestic cats to conservation measures protecting endangered wild cats. Together, they show how a simple roadside warning can be made more memorable while addressing a very real problem.
Article Summary: Japan installs warning signs featuring cats to warn drivers about cats. The playful designs are based on a real danger for cats. Cats can suddenly enter roads while chasing birds or insects. Their sensitivity to noise and light can sometimes cause them to freeze when confronted by a vehicle.

Article Title: Soon, Aussies could opt out of social media algorithms
Article Text:
Australians could be given the option of opting out of powerful social media algorithms.

Australians could be given the option of opting out of powerful social media algorithms under new legislation cracking down on big tech, a minister said Monday. The draft law requiring a “digital duty of care” is expected to be introduced to Australia’s parliament this week.It would require firms like Meta to give users the option of turning off algorithms that tailor recommendations to their personal taste.“A lot of Australians appreciate the algorithm, both for the enjoyment they get out of it or the utility they get out of it,” communications minister Anika Wells told national broadcaster ABC. “A lot of Australians will want to choose the algorithm -- but we think that big tech should offer them the choice in the first place, and they should respect that choice.”“We should give Australians more choice over what they should see on their feeds,” she said.Social media firms have long faced scrutiny over their use of allegedly addictive algorithms and stand accused of directing users to sensational or extreme content to keep them scrolling. Australia implemented legislation barring children from social media platforms in Dec, part of a world-first crackdown designed to protect children from online bullying and “predatory algorithms”.The UK, France and others have followed suit. Data last month found that under-16s in Australia were increasing their use of social m­e­dia apps such as Instagram and TikTok despite the ban.
Article Summary: A draft law requiring a “digital duty of care’ is expected to be introduced to Australia’s parliament this week. It would require firms like Meta to give users the option of turning off algorithms that tailor recommendations to their personal taste. Australia implemented legislation barring children from social media platforms in Dec.

Article Title: A 3,000-year-old ship-shaped stone grave was discovered in Sweden; four urns inside contained burnt human bones and a metal object
Article Text:

Ancient ship-shaped stone grave discovered near Domsten

PC: Svenska kraftnät

How archaeologists estimated the age of the ancient remains

X-rays reveal burnt bones inside four ancient burial urns

What could further examination reveal about the Domsten graves

Archaeologists discovered a prehistoric burial site near Domsten, north of Helsingborg, while monitoring work to replace the Öresund cables. The discovery includes a stone structure shaped like a small ship, measuring about three metres long, as well as two circular stone structures. Four burial urns were also recovered from the site. X-ray images later showed burnt bones and a metal object in one of them. As per Sweden’s national transmission system operator (Svenska kraftnät), they are around 2,500 to 3,000 years old, which places them in the earlier Bronze Age or the early Pre-Roman Iron Age. Archaeologists discovered the site while monitoring work in an area where earlier graves had also been found. Further examination is planned for the autumn that could provide new clues about the people buried there.The discovery was made during archaeological monitoring carried out in connection with Svenska kraftnät’s work on the Öresund cables. Archaeologists initially uncovered flint remains linked to older settlements. They later discovered a stone structure hidden beneath what appeared to be an ordinary stone mound.The structure consisted of a small, ship-shaped stone setting measuring around three metres in length. Two circular stone structures were also found alongside it. Archaeologists believe the site may originally have been covered with earth or peat, creating a low burial mound.The human remains have not yet undergone a full analysis, so archaeologists have estimated their age from the form and construction of the graves. The burial structures suggest that they belong to the earlier part of the Bronze Age or the transition to the Pre-Roman Iron Age, which places the remains roughly 2,500 to 3,000 years old.The discovery also adds to the archaeological evidence from the surrounding area. A separate group of graves found nearby in 2019 was dated to approximately 1400 to 1050 BC. The two discoveries are located around 100 metres apart.Four burial urns were recovered during the excavation. The vessels were described as very well preserved and were almost completely intact when archaeologists removed them from the site. Their condition made it possible to remove all four as a whole for further examination. The urns were subsequently examined using X-rays. The images revealed burnt bones inside the vessels, along with a metal object in one of them. The findings indicate that the urns contain material that can now be studied in greater detail.Reportedly, archaeologists will examine the recovered material in greater detail, including the burial urns and their contents. The preserved bones may provide information about the people buried at the site, including estimates of their age and sex. Researchers will also examine the metal object identified by the X-rays and look for other possible grave goods. The discovery has also raised questions about the wider burial landscape around Domsten.

X-ray images later showed burnt bones and a metal object in one of them. Article Title: In 2024, a Chilean recycling manager deployed discarded salon hair in four booms and one mat in Laguna Verde; about a month later, the devices had reportedly trapped 15 kg of pollutants
Article Text:
AI Representation: Discarded hair forms floating booms and mats that trap pollutants in Laguna Verde. Image credits: Chatgpt

Turning salon sweepings into environmental tools

Why hair works as an oil and metal absorbent

A method already proven around the world

International Coastal cleanup. Image credits: Wikimedia Commons

Scaling beyond a single stream

What the Laguna Verde result suggests going forward

In 2024, Mattia Carenini, who serves as the general manager of Matter of Trust Chile, used Petropelo hair booms in a stream located in Laguna Verde, which is a small town adjacent to Valparaíso, a coastal city. The greywater in the area contained oil and heavy metal pollutants from households and other businesses in the vicinity, and it was draining into the sea, thus providing an ideal scenario for testing a process that uses an extensively studied yet under-utilized property of hair, that is, its ability to soak up oil and heavy metals. In one month, as per the statement by Carenini, the booms collected 15 kg of pollutants from the water that flowed through them, according to El País, without independent verification from other sources.The Matter of Trust Chile organization works in partnership with hairdressing salons and pet-grooming firms across the country in order to collect hair which, otherwise, would have been disposed of as garbage. This organization runs two main projects based on the use of the above-mentioned natural material, namely Petropelo, tube-shaped booms made of hair netting for trapping oil in lakes, rivers, and ocean waters, and Agropelo, hair mats used on agricultural land to reduce evaporation and save irrigation water.According to the description of the Laguna Verde project provided by Matter of Trust itself, the booms used here were made solely from salon and pet-groomer hair.The science behind the technique rests on hair's composition. Human and animal hair is naturally oleophilic, meaning it attracts oil and hydrocarbons while resisting water absorption, which gives it a high capacity to remove pollutants from water without becoming waterlogged itself. The mesh booms installed at Laguna Verde were left in place for about a month, giving the hair enough time to absorb oil and heavy metals through direct contact with the greywater.This idea has already been tested in other cases. According to El País, in its description of the project, hair booms have been applied to solve the issue of oil spills throughout the world, such as the MV Wakashio oil spill, which occurred in 2020 due to the grounding of the ship off the shore of Mauritius, which is one of the notable cases where hair booms were applied. Matter of Trust, the U.S.-based nonprofit that launched the Chilean chapter, has worked on hair booms for many years.Part of what makes the Laguna Verde project notable is where the raw material comes from. As Luisiana Gil, a pet groomer from Santiago, put it, she was regularly throwing out bins full of her customers’ dog hair with nothing to do with them other than to throw them out at the dumpsite. The connection between the hair thrown out and the booms created by Matter of Trust Chile meant giving the useless hair a second life as an instrument of cleaning polluted water. Carenini has talked about their larger aim in the same incremental way, saying that the organization is restoring the site step by step.The organization believes that the amount of hair obtained from one person can be used to clean thousands of liters of water through the use of booms, which highlights the wastage of such absorbent materials in the form of hair that is considered worthless in many salons. Matter of Trust Chile, established in June 2020, is a nonprofit organization that has been identified by the Chilean government as an Institution of Public Interest. It continues to expand its network of partner salons. According to the organization's own site, its mission is to support farmers, fishers, and coastal communities in keeping water clean while regenerating soil.But while a 15-kilogram performance figure based only on one month’s effort at one location does not prove that hair booms can combat industrial-scale pollution, it does indicate that it is possible to see an effect from using a low-cost material made entirely out of waste produced in another industry. Whether the technique can scale up for larger or more polluted locations is still an open question and will probably depend upon the number of Chilean beauty and grooming salons that choose to donate their waste to Matter of Trust.
Article Summary: Hair is naturally oleophilic, meaning it attracts oil and hydrocarbons while resisting water absorption. This gives it a high capacity to remove pollutants from water without becoming waterlogged itself. Matter of Trust Chile, a U.S.-based nonprofit, works with salons and pet groomers across the country to create hair booms. The booms collected 15 kg of pollutants from the water that flowed through them.

Article Title: Rwanda planted dozens of exotic tree species in an experimental forest in 1933; 90 years later scientists found eucalyptus had acidified the soil
Article Text:
Image AI generated

Eucalyptus became Rwanda’s dominant plantation tree

Scientists raised concerns about eucalyptus and soil

Image AI generated

Researchers measured eucalyptus water use in southern Rwanda

In Rwanda, an experiment with exotic trees grew into a much larger forestry programme, with eucalyptus eventually becoming the country’s dominant plantation tree. A 200-hectare arboretum was established at Ruhande in Butare to test exotic species, including 63 species of eucalyptus, as Rwanda prepared to expand plantation forestry. By the early 1970s, eucalyptus plantations in Rwanda had reached about 23,000 hectares, part of a wider 95,684-hectare area across several East African countries. The expansion also brought questions about what intensive eucalyptus planting could mean for the environment. Researchers have examined concerns ranging from nutrient removal and soil quality to water use. According to the study published in Springer Nature Link, titled ‘ Water use by short rotation Eucalyptus woodlots in southern Rwanda ’, eucalyptus has been described as taking up large amounts of nutrients, potentially leaving soils poorer for other uses. However, the available research does not establish a 90-year soil-acidification finding at Ruhande, and the study discussed here focuses primarily on eucalyptus water use in southern Rwanda.The experiment was followed by a much wider expansion of eucalyptus planting. By the early 1970s, eucalyptus plantations across Ethiopia, Rwanda, Uganda, Kenya and Sudan covered 95,684 hectares, with Rwanda accounting for about 23,000 hectares at the time.The supplied paper notes that Rwanda and Ethiopia had the largest areas among those countries.In Rwanda itself, eucalyptus became the dominant plantation tree. The study states that eucalyptus accounted for 78% of forest plantations, with most plantations managed as short-rotation coppice. Small woodlots were particularly common, often appearing as groups or rows of trees scattered across farmland.The environmental effects of eucalyptus planting were already an area of scientific discussion. The supplied source notes that some researchers supported eucalyptus plantations for their economic, social and environmental benefits, while other research raised concerns about their effects on soil. In particular, it reports that eucalyptus had been described as taking up substantial quantities of nutrients, potentially leaving soils poorer for subsequent uses.The paper does not, however, report a 90-year comparison showing that eucalyptus at Ruhande acidified the soil. Its own research examined water use by short-rotation eucalyptus woodlots in southern Rwanda, rather than measuring a century-long change in soil acidity. The source cites a separate 2009 study titled Soil CO2 flux in six monospecific forest plantations in Southern Rwanda, but the supplied material does not provide that study's soil-pH results.The researchers examined eucalyptus woodlots in the Butare and Busoro catchments in southern Rwanda. The study found that the stands were generally small, frequently coppiced plantations, with tree diameters ranging from 2 to 36 centimetres. Potential tree transpiration ranged from 0.41 to 6.44 millimetres per day in the Busoro catchment and from 1.34 to 3.44 millimetres per day in the Butare catchment.The study's overall estimate was about 3 millimetres of potential tree transpiration per day, or roughly 1,095 millimetres per year. Long-term precipitation at the study site averaged 1,245 millimetres annually, and those dry-season water deficits could be reduced through lower leaf area and stomatal closure. The paper therefore concluded that the short-rotation woodlots studied did not necessarily produce a negative annual water balance.
Article Summary: Eucalyptus plantations in Rwanda had reached about 23,000 hectares by the early 1970s, part of a wider 95,684-hectare area across several East African countries. Researchers have examined concerns ranging from nutrient removal and soil quality to water use. The study concluded that short-rotation woodlots studied did not necessarily produce a negative annual water balance.

Article Title: In 1974, a California college student built a cabin using only hand tools because his father said, ‘no electricity’; 52 years later, it sits inside a $6M estate with a runway, helipad and 82-ft pool
Article Text:
Pic credit: Sacbee

From a hand-built cabin to an empire

Pic credit: Sacbee

What the buyer gets

Pic credit: Sacbee

Pic credit: Sacbee

Pic credit: Sacbee

Kenneth Roebbelen’s luxury estate now features a 9,800-sq-ft main house, along with a 2,200-sq-ft recreation centre, an 82-ft Junior Olympic lap pool, a private runway, an aircraft hangar and a helipad, the Sacramento Bee reported. But half a century ago, this sprawling property in the Sacramento area looked different. It started with a small cabin, completely built using hand tools.Kenneth Roebbelen’s father, Hans Roebbelen, bought the Sacramento-area estate in the late 1960s. In 1974, Kenneth Roebbelen graduated from UC Davis; he wanted to avoid dorm living. So when he started to build a cabin, his father had one condition attached to it, which made the project part construction job and part character test.“The rule was I had to only use hand tools, no power tools, no electricity,” Roebbelen said. During weekends, he would come over to build the cabin, so he would have a place to live instead of renting an apartment after college. The 1974 cabin stands even today and is now part of the complex that grew with Roebbelen’s career, family and landholding. Kenneth Roebbelen is the former president of his family-owned Roebbelen Contracting Inc., founded by his father, Hans Roebbelen, in 1959. The family eventually owned 623 acres of land stretching to Folsom Lake. Today, the gated estate in El Dorado Hills covers 48 acres and is on the market for $6 million.Roebbelen raised three children with his wife, Kimberly, in homes built gradually around that original hand-built cabin. The main residence was built between 2008 and 2010. The pool house and the pool arrived in 2024. The trick, he said, was making each era look like it belonged to the others all along. “You’re doing all this stuff in different phases of your life, and part of the goal is to make it look like it was done at one time. That it was all coordinated,” he told the outlet.This aesthetic is also deeply woven into the physical fabric. The main residence features cherrywood ceilings, Brazilian cherry floors, hydronically heated floors and carved mahogany double doors. A staircase rises more than 40 feet; carved mahogany double doors open into foyers flooded with light, and hydronically heated floors are fitted beneath it all. The primary suite has dual walk-in closets. It comes with a soaking tub, steam shower, dry sauna and private fitness area.The main entrance has wrought-iron double doors leading into an elaborate foyer with a soaring ceiling and custom stone floors. There is an art gallery that runs through the house and connects its different sections: the original cabin, older portions and the newer main house upstairs.The most striking feature is something else: mahogany wine cellar doors, intricately carved in Monterrey, Mexico, lead to a cellar that can house 2,300 bottles. A freezer salvaged from Sacramento High School’s renovation when Roebbelen was still in high school now serves as the walk-in refrigerator. It’s nearly a century old, according to him.The unique estate also has a 9,800-square-foot main residence, a 2,200-square-foot pool house anchored by an 82-foot Junior Olympic lap pool, a spring-fed fishing pond, an airstrip with a hangar, a helipad and enough amenities to rival a small resort.There is a six-car garage, storage for RVs and boats, and also a massive fertile garden built during the COVID-19 pandemic. It is nothing less than a commercial-grade greenhouse.Bronze mustangs titled ‘Spirit of Nevada’ greet visitors at the entry gate, a work by Auburn sculptor Doug Van Howd. There’s more art across the estate. For instance, a striking statue of a woman dressed in a white dress, created by Ken Shutt, overlooks the water of the expanded pond.A solar system producing 38 kilowatts, paired with ten Tesla batteries, generally offsets the property’s electricity consumption, though the pool house occasionally tips the balance. A metal roof, extensive stonework and granite hardscape speak to investment beyond the visual. The runway his father installed as an avid pilot remains; when Roebbelen ran the construction company, it let him reach Western jobs and return home the same day via pilot project managers.Beyond its size and resort-level amenities, the kind of work that’s nearly impossible to replicate at current costs, let alone afford. According to the listing agent, the $6 million asking price is a great deal. “To build this today would be $15 million. I mean, you couldn’t do it. It is absolutely worth every nickel,” listing agent Chris Wolfe of eXp Realty told the outlet.
Article Summary: Kenneth Roebbelen’s luxury estate now features a 9,800-sq-ft main house, along with a 2,200- sq-ft recreation centre, an 82-ft Junior Olympic lap pool, a private runway, an aircraft hangar and a helipad. But half a century ago, this sprawling property in the Sacramento area looked different. It started with a small cabin, completely built using hand tools.

Article Title: Meet Andy Barrett, the 13-year-old Ohio student who turned a school 3D printer into a small business, selling 150 fidget toys and raising money for epilepsy awareness
Article Text:
Photo: Andy BarrettPhoto credit: https://lp.constantcontactpages.com

From classroom tool to business idea

Designing and printing the toys

Selling 150 fidget toys

Why epilepsy awareness?

Profits into impact

Support from school and family

What’s next for Andy?

Most 13-year-olds walk into middle school tech lab thinking about passing their next assignment or making something cool to toss into their backpack. Andy Barrett, an eighth-grader at Granville Middle School in Ohio, saw something entirely different when he looked at his school's 3D printer. He saw an opportunity to build a business that could actually help people. Armed with basic design software, brightly colored plastic filament, and a personal drive to make a difference, Andy launched a micro-business right from his classroom. He designed, printed, and sold roughly 150 custom fidget toys to fellow students, teachers, and neighbours. Instead of pocketing the money for video games or new shoes, he directed every cent of his profits toward epilepsy awareness and research.The project began inside a standard technology and engineering class, the kind of room where students typically learn the basics of digital design and manufacturing. In most middle schools, a 3D printer gets used to produce simple trinkets, small keychains, or prototype parts for short-term grading rubrics. Andy realised early on that the technology offered far more potential.He noticed how popular fidget toys had become among his peers. Kids were constantly looking for tactile objects to help them focus, manage stress, or simply keep their hands occupied during long school days. Rather than buying mass-produced plastic toys from big store shelves, Andy figured he could design his own versions, customise them, and offer them directly to people around him.Bringing a digital design to life takes far more work than simply hitting print. After getting approval from his teachers, Andy spent long hours in the school lab perfecting his fidget toys. He learnt the software from scratch, playing around with different shapes, hinges and textures, so the finished pieces felt comfortable to hold. The learning curve was sharp. He'd tackle clogged nozzles, peeling plastic, and failed prints tossed into the scrap bin. After printing, each piece required a bit of handwork, like trimming away excess material or smoothing out any rough spots. Andy relied on his friends to test early prototypes, modifying his designs according to their feedback until the toys were rugged and dependable.When the other kids saw the bright, custom toys in action, word spread through the hallways in a hurry. What began as a few casual sales has turned into a steady stream of orders, with teachers, school staff and neighbours getting in on the act. Andy quickly found himself running a real business, keeping track of customers and money, fitting in printing time around his classes. When he finally hit his goal of selling 150 toys, he had built a functioning, thriving business right out of his middle school science lab.What truly set Andy apart was his motivation. From the very beginning, he decided that the proceeds would go directly to funding epilepsy research and supporting organisations that help families dealing with the condition. The choice was deeply personal. Andy knows people in his life who have epilepsy, a neurological disorder that causes unpredictable, recurring seizures. Seeing friends or family struggle with the difficulties of the condition gave him a clear view that it can be hard. In addition to the physical toll of medical appointments and daily medications, people with epilepsy often face social stigma, anxiety and a general lack of understanding from those around them. Andy saw his fidget toys as a creative way to start conversations, educate his peers and create meaningful support for a cause that doesn’t get enough attention in middle school halls.Andy turned profits into donations and simple plastic gadgets into tools for social good. While the dollar figure alone was an impressive accomplishment for an eighth-grader, the educational impact went so much deeper. Every transaction became a moment to talk about epilepsy. Classmates who bought a toy were not just getting a fun accessory for their desk, they were learning about a neurological condition that affects millions of children and adults worldwide. Andy proved that you do not need a massive corporate budget to make a meaningful difference in your community.Projects like this rarely succeed in a vacuum. Andy’s initiative flourished because his surrounding community chose to champion his effort. His teachers provided the trust, classroom access, and flexibility needed to run the 3D printers during free hours. His family helped him plan the sales, manage the money responsibly and donate the proceeds to real non-profits. His friends and neighbours showed up as excited customers. This collaborative spirit shows what’s possible when schools and communities support young people to pursue true passion projects.Andy is 13 years old and still in middle school. He has many years of learning and experimentation ahead of him. He could keep selling fidget toys. He could expand into other 3D-printed products. Or he could channel his energy into new causes and new projects. Whatever he does next, he’ll take experience of running a small, purpose-led company with him. The 150 fidget toys he sold and the money he raised for epilepsy awareness are real proof right now that even one student can use a classroom tool for good, if he has the right support and motivation. Armed with basic design software, brightly colored plastic filament, and a personal drive to make a difference, Andy launched a micro-business. He designed, printed, and sold roughly 150 custom fidget toys to fellow students, teachers, and neighbours.

Article Title: Meet Benjamin Choi, a 17-year-old who built a $300 mind-controlled prosthetic arm that reads brainwaves through non-invasive electrodes
Article Text: Each one of us spent the pandemic doing something that we normally wouldn't have the time to. While some picked up numerous indoor hobbies, others studied hard enough to change career pathways. Benjamin Choi, a then 17-year-old kid, put his spare time during the phase to design an accessible device that does not require brain surgery.When he was in third grade, Choi watched a "60 Minutes" documentary about a mind-controlled prosthesis. Researchers implanted tiny sensors into the motor cortex of the brain of a patient who moved a robotic arm using her thoughts. “I was really, really amazed at the time because this technology was so impressive,” he said to Smithsonian Magazine. “But I was also alarmed that they require this really risky open brain surgery. And they're so inaccessible, costing in the hundreds of thousands of dollars.”Years later, when the pandemic hit in 2020, Choi, a tenth grader living in Virginia found himself with ample free time. The lab in which he’d planned to spend his summer researching aluminium fuels had shut down. But the documentary he had seen years earlier stuck with him, and he decided to use his spare time to build a less-invasive prosthetic arm himself.He formed a makeshift laboratory on the ping-pong table in his basement and designed the first version of his robotic arm using his sister's $75 3D printer and some fishing line. The printer couldn’t build pieces over 4.7 inches in length, so Choi printed the arm in tiny pieces and bolted and rubber-banded it together. In total, it took about 30 hours to print. This version worked using brain wave data and head gestures, and Choi posted instructions online for anyone to build their own.He had some previous experience building robots and coding from participating in competitive robotics at the elementary, middle school and high school levels, even going to the world championships several times. Starting in ninth grade, he taught himself the computer programming languages Python and C++ by watching videos on Stack Overflow, a website for programmers.After more than 75 design iterations, Choi's non-invasive, mind-controlled robotic arm could be made from engineering-grade materials, able to withstand weights up to about four tons. It operates using an algorithm driven by artificial intelligence (A.I.) that interprets a user’s brain waves. And it only costs around $300 to manufacture—a huge savings compared to what’s currently on the market. A more basic, body-powered upper limb prosthesis costs about $7,000. As of 2015, the very advanced, full-arm Modular Prosthetic Limb, which has 26 joints, hundreds of sensors and can curl up to 45 pounds, cost about $500,000. This prosthesis, paired with a surgery to reroute nerves that once controlled the arm, allows patients to command the limb with their thoughts and even feel texture through it.Choi’s arm uses electroencephalography, or EEG, to avoid the invasive techniques of other prostheses. EEG devices record the brain’s electrical activity using sensors placed on the head. They are often used in medicine to diagnose epilepsy or other brain disorders. His system uses two electrodes: a baseline sensor that clips onto the earlobe and another on the forehead that collects EEG data. The forehead electrode picks up brain wave information, which is sent to a microchip in the prosthetic arm via Bluetooth. An A.I. model that Choi created, also embedded in the chip, deciphers the data and converts it into a prediction of what the brain is thinking. The arm also moves using head gestures and stops with intentional blinks.The invention earned Choi a spot in the top 40 finalists of 2022's Regeneron Science Talent Search, America's oldest and most prestigious science and math competition for high school seniors. “It means a lot to me to see that my work is recognised like this,” Choi said at the time. “I'm definitely very grateful to be a finalist.” The young inventor went on to win funding from the Massachusetts Institute of Technology in 2021 to continue his research and work with experts at the university. For about six months, he experimented with cloud computing to make the arm internet-compatible. To create his A.I. model, he worked independently with six adult volunteers for about two hours each, collecting their brain wave data at his school and home. While collecting the data via an electrode on the forehead, he asked each participant to focus on clenching and unclenching their hand. He trained the A.I. to distinguish between the brain signals, and the A.I. model continuously learns from a user’s brain waves. In total, the algorithm has over 23,000 lines of code, with 978 pages of math and seven completely new sub-algorithms. Choi’s algorithm performs with a mean accuracy of 95 per cent. He said the previous gold standard for a similar artificial neural network was 73.8 per cent.In 2021, he was selected as a Simons Fellow at Stony Brook University, where he worked remotely with Ji Liu, a professor in the department of electrical and computer engineering, on the machine learning algorithm of his AI. Choi has also won awards in the Regeneron International Science and Engineering Fair, the Microsoft Imagine Cup, and the National At-Home STEM Competition. He received a manufacturing grant in October 2020 from PolySpectra, Inc. , a company that produces durable 3-D printed materials, to produce his arm.Over the past few years, Choi has only furthered his achievements. In 2023, he did machine learning research at The Johns Hopkins University Applied Physics Laboratory. From August to December 2024, he worked as a researcher with NASA and currently works as an AI researcher at the Kempner Institute at Harvard University. He is about to graduate with a degree in applied math and a concurrent master's in computer science from the Harvard John A. Paulson School of Engineering and Applied Sciences.The bionic arm, whose underlying signal processing he continued developing at Johns Hopkins, was the foundation of Choi’s interests. But his time at SEAS, whether with the Weber Group or Kempner Institute, has both broadened and refined his understanding of machine learning. Now set to enter the workforce, Choi is fully ready to continue what he’s always done: find ways to apply his research in the world around him.
Article Summary: Benjamin Choi, a tenth grader living in Virginia, has designed a mind-controlled robotic arm that does not require brain surgery. Choi's arm uses electroencephalography, or EEG, to avoid the invasive techniques of other prostheses. It operates using an algorithm driven by artificial intelligence (A.I.) that interprets a user’s brain waves.

Article Title: Nominee vs legal heir: What is the difference and who has claim on assets? All you need to know
Article Text:
AI image

Who is a Nominee?



Who is a Legal Heir?

Difference between a Nominee and a Legal heir

Aspect Nominee Legal Heir Role Custodian Owner Transfer of Assets Can be done without any legal formalities. Requires testamentary documents for proof of ownership. Powers No power to transact, use, or transfer assets. Power to use and transact assets as an owner. Appointment Owner can appoint anyone, but some institutions specify certain conditions. Determined by succession/personal laws. Legal Right Cannot contest ownership legally. Can contest ownership in a court of law.

When individuals open bank accounts, invest in mutual funds, or buy insurance, they are often asked to name a nominee.However, many people mistakenly assume that the nominee automatically inherits the assets. In reality, the nominee is not always the final recipient — the ownership rights belong to the legal heir, reported ET.Understanding the distinction between these two is essential to ensure that your wealth is passed on to the intended beneficiaries.A nominee acts as a temporary custodian of the deceased person’s assets.The nominee’s role is limited to holding and managing the assets until they are legally transferred to the rightful heirs.According to ET, the nominee cannot sell, trade, or make any transactional decisions about the assets.The account or policy owner can appoint anyone — family, friends, or acquaintances — as a nominee, though financial institutions often prefer close family members.In some cases, the nominee and the legal heir can be the same person, which helps in ensuring a smoother transfer of assets.The legal heir or beneficiary is the rightful owner of the assets once the original holder passes away.To claim ownership, the legal heir must produce valid documents such as a will or other testamentary proof.If there is no will — a situation known as dying intestate — the heir is determined as per the country’s succession or personal laws, reported ET.While a nominee can initially access the assets, only the legal heir can claim them permanently or challenge ownership in court.Experts quoted by ET emphasise that having clarity on this difference helps avoid disputes and ensures that the savings reach the intended family members or beneficiaries.Therefore, it is advisable to regularly update both nominees and wills to align with one’s estate planning goals.
Article Summary: A nominee acts as a temporary custodian of the deceased person’s assets. The legal heir or beneficiary is the rightful owner of the assets once the original holder passes away. To claim ownership, the legal heir must produce valid documents such as a will.

How Jeevan Pramaan simplifies pensioner verification



Every year, lakhs of pensioners across India must prove that they are still alive to continue receiving their pension. This verification, known as the Life Certificate or Digital Life Certificate (DLC), is a crucial and mandatory step in ensuring that pension payments are made only to eligible recipients, preventing fraud and misuse.Traditionally, this process involved visiting the bank or pension office in person, standing in long queues, and submitting a signed paper certificate. However, with the government’s focus on digitisation and technological advancement, this process has become much simpler, faster, and more convenient. Pensioners can now submit their certificates digitally from the comfort of their homes using Jeevan Pramaan, a secure, user-friendly, and Aadhaar-based platform.A Life Certificate is an official document that confirms a pensioner is alive. Without it, pension payments are automatically paused by the pension disbursing agency. This verification is essential for preventing fraudulent claims and ensuring that pensions reach the rightful beneficiaries.The Digital Life Certificate (DLC), also known as Jeevan Pramaan, is an advanced biometric-enabled version of the traditional paper certificate.Introduced by the Government of India, it uses Aadhaar-based biometric authentication using either fingerprint or iris scan to verify a pensioner’s identity. Once verified, a digital certificate is automatically generated and shared with authorised pension disbursing agencies.This online process eliminates the need for physical verification, providing elderly pensioners with a simpler and more accessible way to maintain their pension benefits.According to PIB, The submission of the Life Certificate is mandatory for all pensioners who wish to continue receiving their pension without interruption. For the year 2025, the standard submission period is betweenTo make the process more comfortable for the elderly, the government allows pensioners aged 80 years and above to begin the submission process earlier, from 1 October 2025. This extended window gives senior citizens more time and flexibility to complete the procedure without facing last-minute difficulties.The Jeevan Pramaan process involves two main steps: registering the biometric device and generating the digital certificate.Before using the service, pensioners or operators must register their biometric device such as a fingerprint or iris scanner. During registration, the user provides their Aadhaar number and mobile number, after which an OTP (One-Time Password) is sent to their mobile. After entering the OTP, they must provide their name and email ID before scanning their fingerprint or iris.Once authentication is complete, the system confirms that device registration was successful, allowing the user to move to the next step.In this step, the pensioner enters personal details such as Aadhaar number, mobile number, name, PPO number, pension type, sanctioning authority, disbursing agency, and bank account details. The system also asks whether the pensioner has remarried or is re-employed.After entering all details, the pensioner scans their fingerprint or iris using the registered biometric device. Upon successful authentication, the Digital Life Certificate is generated, and an SMS acknowledgment with the Jeevan Pramaan Certificate ID is sent to the registered mobile number.This certificate is automatically stored in the Life Certificate Repository, accessible anytime to both pensioners and pension agencies.Once the Digital Life Certificate is created, it can be electronically delivered to the concerned Pension Disbursing Agency (PDA). PDAs can log in to the Jeevan Pramaan portal to view, verify, or download the certificate directly.Pensioners can also download a PDF copy of their certificate by visiting the Jeevan Pramaan website and entering their Pramaan ID or Aadhaar number. This ensures transparency and easy access for future reference.The government provides several options to submit the Life Certificate, allowing pensioners to choose the method that suits them best.Pensioners who prefer traditional methods can visit their bank branch or a Citizen Service Centre (CSC) to submit their Life Certificate physically. Trained staff at these centres assist pensioners in verifying their details and completing the process.For those unable to travel due to age or health issues, India Post Payments Bank (IPPB) offers a doorstep banking service. Pensioners can schedule an appointment, and an IPPB representative will visit their home to complete the submission using biometric authentication. This service is available for both IPPB and non-IPPB account holders.For pensioners comfortable with technology, the Jeevan Pramaan portal provides a completely online process. By visiting https://jeevanpramaan.gov.in, pensioners can submit their Digital Life Certificate using a computer, laptop, or smartphone equipped with a fingerprint or iris scanner.The system uses the Aadhaar platform to authenticate biometric details. Once verification is successful, a Digital Life Certificate is generated and stored in a secure online repository. Pension disbursing agencies can then directly access the certificate, removing the need for physical paperwork.The UMANG (Unified Mobile Application for New-age Governance) app offers another easy option. Pensioners can download the app from the Google Play Store, search for “Jeevan Pramaan,” and select “Generate Life Certificate.”After entering the necessary details such as Aadhaar number, PPO number, and type of pension, pensioners must authenticate themselves using biometric verification. The app then generates a Digital Life Certificate (DLC), which is automatically shared with the pension disbursing authority.All pensioners who receive government, defence, or private sector pensions through authorised disbursing agencies are required to submit their Life Certificate every year. This includes:Failure to submit the certificate within the stipulated period may result in temporary suspension of pension payments until verification is completed.To ensure a smooth submission process, pensioners should keep certain details and documents ready. These include:Having these details ready helps to avoid delays or errors during authentication, whether submitting online or offline.Yes, an Aadhaar number or Virtual ID (VID) is mandatory to generate a Digital Life Certificate. The entire Jeevan Pramaan system is based on Aadhaar authentication, which ensures accuracy and prevents fraud. Pensioners must make sure their Aadhaar is linked with their mobile number and bank account before attempting to generate the certificate.The Digital Life Certificate is fully valid and legally recognised under the Information Technology Act. Pension disbursing authorities across India accept it as an official document, equivalent to the traditional paper-based life certificate.Its biometric verification system makes it secure and tamper-proof, reducing the chances of wrongful pension disbursal or misuse of pension funds.Before the introduction of Jeevan Pramaan, pensioners often faced difficulties in submitting their certificates, especially those with health problems or limited mobility. The digital system has removed these challenges, allowing pensioners to submit their verification anytime and anywhere.By integrating biometric technology and Aadhaar authentication, Jeevan Pramaan has streamlined pension management, improving efficiency for both pensioners and government departments. It also enhances transparency and ensures that genuine beneficiaries receive payments on time.

This verification is essential for preventing fraudulent claims and ensuring that pensions reach the rightful beneficiaries. The Digital Life Certificate (DLC), also known as Jeevan Pramaan, is an advanced biometric- enabled version of the traditional paper certificate.
